nodes.statement: thmtitleDecay at infinity The initial data h_0 : R to [-infty, infty) of the KPZ fixed point is a non-random, upper semicontinuous function that is not identically equal to -infty, and for which (a)~there exist alphainR and gamma>0 such that the bound h_0(y) leq alpha - gamma |y|^1/2 holds for all y in R and (b)~there exists lambda in R such that h_0(y) = -infty for yleq -lambda.
nodes.raw_latex:
\thmtitle{Decay at infinity}\label{a:initial_state_pd} 
The initial data $\mathfrak{h}_0 : \mathbb{R} \to [-\infty, \infty)$ of the KPZ fixed point is a non-random, upper semicontinuous function that is not identically equal to $-\infty$, and for which (a)~there exist $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$ and $\gamma>0$ such that the bound $\mathfrak{h}_0(y) \leq \alpha - \gamma |y|^{1/2}$ holds for all $y \in \mathbb{R}$ and (b)~there exists $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$ such that $\mathfrak{h}_0(y) = -\infty$ for $y\leq -\lambda$.

nodes.label: a:initial_state_pd

\label{prop:sym}
Let $\mathfrak{h}_t(x; \mathfrak{h}_0)$ denote the KPZ fixed point with initial data $\mathfrak{h}_0\in \uptext{UC}$. Then it has the following properties, where all of the identities in distribution are for random functions in the spatial variable on $x\in\mathbb{R}$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\normalfont{(\roman*)},ref=\roman*]
\item \label{123a}  \emph{(1:2:3 scaling invariance)} For any $\alpha>0$, one has $\alpha\hspace{0.05em}\mathfrak{h}_{\alpha^{-3}t}(\alpha^{-2}x; \mathfrak{h}^{\alpha}_0)\stackrel{\uptext{\tiny{dist}}}{=} \mathfrak{h}_t(x;\mathfrak{h}_0)$ as a process in both $x$ and $t$, where $\mathfrak{h}^\alpha_0(x) := \alpha^{-1}\mathfrak{h}_0(\alpha^{2}x)$.
\item \label{sis} \emph{(Stationarity in space)} For any $t > 0$ and $u \in \mathbb{R}$, $\mathfrak{h}_t(x +u; \mathfrak{h}_0(\,\mathpalette{\mathpalette{\mathpalette{\mathpalette{\mathpalette{\mathpalette{\mathpalette{\mathpalette\bigcdot@{.5}}@{.5}}@{.5}}@{.5}}@{.5}}@{.5}}@{.5}}@{.5}\, -u))\stackrel{\uptext{\tiny{dist}}}{=} \mathfrak{h}_t(x; \mathfrak{h}_0)$, where we write $\mathfrak{h}_0(\,\mathpalette{\mathpalette{\mathpalette{\mathpalette{\mathpalette{\mathpalette{\mathpalette{\mathpalette\bigcdot@{.5}}@{.5}}@{.5}}@{.5}}@{.5}}@{.5}}@{.5}}@{.5}\, -u)$ for the function $y \mapsto \mathfrak{h}_0(y -u)$.
\item \label{ai} \emph{(Affine invariance)} Let $\mathfrak{f}(x) = \mathfrak{h}_0(x) + a + c x$ for some constants $a, c$. Then one has $\mathfrak{h}_t(x; \mathfrak{f})\stackrel{\uptext{\tiny{dist}}}{=} \mathfrak{h}_t(x+\frac12ct; \mathfrak{h}_0) + a + cx + \frac14c^2t$ as a process in $x$ and $t$.
\item  \label{str} \emph{(Skew time reversibility)} For any functions $\mathfrak{f},\mathfrak{g}\in\uptext{UC}$,
\begin{equation}
\mathbb P\big(\mathfrak{h}_t(x; \mathfrak{g})\le -\mathfrak{f}(x), \,\forall\,x \in \mathbb{R}\big) =\mathbb P\big(\mathfrak{h}_t(x;\mathfrak{f})\le -\mathfrak{g}(x), \,\forall\,x \in \mathbb{R}\big).
\end{equation}
\item \label{pom} \emph{(Preservation of max)} For any $\mathfrak{f}_1,\mathfrak{f}_2\in\uptext{UC}$ and $t > 0$, the KPZ fixed points $\mathfrak{h}_t(\mathpalette{\mathpalette{\mathpalette{\mathpalette{\mathpalette{\mathpalette{\mathpalette{\mathpalette\bigcdot@{.5}}@{.5}}@{.5}}@{.5}}@{.5}}@{.5}}@{.5}}@{.5}\,; \mathfrak{f}_1)$ and $\mathfrak{h}_t(\mathpalette{\mathpalette{\mathpalette{\mathpalette{\mathpalette{\mathpalette{\mathpalette{\mathpalette\bigcdot@{.5}}@{.5}}@{.5}}@{.5}}@{.5}}@{.5}}@{.5}}@{.5}\,; \mathfrak{f}_2)$ can be coupled so that $\mathfrak{h}_t(x; \mathfrak{f}_1)\vee \mathfrak{h}_t(x; \mathfrak{f}_2) \stackrel{\uptext{\tiny{dist}}}{=} \mathfrak{h}_t(x;\mathfrak{f}_1\vee \mathfrak{f}_2)$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$.
\item \label{mon} \emph{(Monotonicity)} For any $t > 0$ and $\mathfrak{f}_1,\mathfrak{f}_2\in\uptext{UC}$ such that $\mathfrak{f}_1 \geq \mathfrak{f}_2$, the KPZ fixed points $\mathfrak{h}_t(\mathpalette{\mathpalette{\mathpalette{\mathpalette{\mathpalette{\mathpalette{\mathpalette{\mathpalette\bigcdot@{.5}}@{.5}}@{.5}}@{.5}}@{.5}}@{.5}}@{.5}}@{.5}\,; \mathfrak{f}_1)$ and $\mathfrak{h}_t(\mathpalette{\mathpalette{\mathpalette{\mathpalette{\mathpalette{\mathpalette{\mathpalette{\mathpalette\bigcdot@{.5}}@{.5}}@{.5}}@{.5}}@{.5}}@{.5}}@{.5}}@{.5}\,; \mathfrak{f}_2)$ can be coupled so that $\mathfrak{h}_t(x;\mathfrak{f}_1) \geq \mathfrak{h}_t(x; \mathfrak{f}_2)$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$ a.s.\
\item \label{space} \emph{($\tfrac{1}{2}^{{\scriptscriptstyle-}}-$H\"older regularity in space)} For any fixed $t>0$ and $\beta\in (0,\tfrac12)$, the function $x \mapsto \mathfrak{h}_t(x; \mathfrak{h}_0)$ is almost surely locally $\beta$-H\"{o}lder continuous.
\item \label{time} \emph{($\tfrac{1}{3}^{{\scriptscriptstyle-}}$-H\"older regularity in time)} For any fixed $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and $\beta\in (0,\tfrac13)$, the function $t \mapsto \mathfrak{h}_t(x; \mathfrak{h}_0)$ is almost surely locally $\beta$-H\"{o}lder continuous.
\end{enumerate}

nodes.statement: For any initial data h_0 satisfying Assumption~(a) and for any T > 0, there exists a random variable B in R, which is almost surely finite, such that the KPZ fixed point h_t satisfies h_t(x) leq B - frac18minleft(sqrt2gamma, frac1tright) |x|^1/2, for all x in R and t in [0, T], where the constant gamma > 0 is from Assumption~. In particular, for every fixed t geq 0, the KPZ fixed point h_t(x) is almost surely bounded above, and lim_x to pm infty h_t(x) = -infty almost surely.

We first observe that, by the continuity of $(t,x)\mapsto \mathfrak{h}_t(x)$, it is enough to prove \eqref{eq:KPZ_is_bounded} under the assumption that $|x|\geq 1$.

We will use the variational formula \eqref{eq:variational} and properties of the directed landscape. Let us fix some $\delta>0$ and denote $F_\delta(y, s, x, t) := \mathcal{C}_\delta (1 + \Vert y, s, x, t \Vert^{1 / 5})$, where $\Vert \mathpalette{\mathpalette{\mathpalette{\mathpalette{\mathpalette{\mathpalette{\mathpalette{\mathpalette\bigcdot@{.5}}@{.5}}@{.5}}@{.5}}@{.5}}@{.5}}@{.5}}@{.5} \Vert$ is the $\ell_1$-norm on $\mathbb{R}^4$ and $\mathcal{C}_\delta$ is the $\delta$-dependent random variable from \eqref{eq:Landscape_bound1}, which is positive and almost surely finite. Then, for any $(y, s; x, t) \in \mathbb{R}^4_{\uparrow}$, \eqref{eq:Landscape_bound1} yields

\begin{equation}\label{eq:Landscape_bound2}
- F_\delta(y, s, x, t) (t-s)^{\frac{1}{3} - \delta} - \tfrac{(x-y)^2}{t-s} \leq \mathcal{L}(y, s; x, t) \leq F_\delta(y, s, x, t) (t-s)^{\frac{1}{3} - \delta} - \tfrac{(x-y)^2}{t-s}.
\end{equation}

Since we are going to use $F_\delta$ and $\mathcal{C}_\delta$ for a fixed value $\delta$, we prefer to make our notation slightly lighter and omit the subscripts $\delta$ in the rest of this proof. From \eqref{eq:variational}, \eqref{eq:Landscape_bound2} and Assumption~\ref{a:initial_state_pd}, we obtain

\begin{equation}\label{eq:KPZ_is_bounded1}
\mathfrak{h}_t(x) \leq \sup_{y \in \mathbb{R}} \Bigl\{ \alpha - \gamma |y|^{1/2} + F(y, 0, x, t) t^{\frac{1}{3} - \delta} - \tfrac{(x-y)^2}{t} \Bigr\}.
\end{equation}

We consider $t \in [0, T]$ for fixed $T > 0$.

We want to upper bound $-\gamma |y|^{1/2}/2 - (x-y)^2/t$ by $-c_{\gamma,t} |x|^{1/2}$ for some $c_{\gamma,t}>0$ for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$. First, by the triangle inequality we have $(x-y)^2/t \geq (|x|-|y|)^2/t$. Next, we write 

$$\frac{\gamma}{2}|y|^{1/2}+\frac{(|x|-|y|)^2}{t} = \frac{\gamma}{2}|y|^{1/2}+|x|^2\frac{(1-|y|/|x|)^2}{t}.$$

If $|y|/|x| \leq 1/2$, we ignore the first term and obtain a lower bound of $|x|^{1/2}/(4t)$, using $|x|^2\geq |x|^{1/2}$since $|x|\geq 1$ by assumption. If $|y|/|x|\geq 1/2$, we ignore the second term and obtain a lower bound of $\gamma |x|^{1/2}/2\sqrt{2}$. Thus we see

$$-\frac{\gamma}{2} |y|^{1/2} - \frac{(x-y)^2}{t} \leq -c_{\gamma,t}|x|^{1/2}$$

with $c_{\gamma,t} = \min(1/(4t), \gamma/2\sqrt{2})$. Substituting this in \eqref{eq:KPZ_is_bounded1}, we obtain

\begin{align*}
\MoveEqLeft[6]
\sup_{y\in\mathbb{R}}\left\{\alpha - \gamma |y|^{1/2} + F(y, 0, x, t) t^{\frac{1}{3} - \delta} - \frac{(x-y)^2}{t}\right\}\\

&\leq \sup_{y\in\mathbb{R}}\left\{\alpha - \frac{\gamma}{2}|y|^{1/2}+F(y, 0, x, t)t^{\frac{1}{3} - \delta} - c_{\gamma,t}|x|^{1/2}\right\}\\

&\leq \sup_{x, y\in\mathbb{R}}\left\{\alpha - \frac{\gamma}{2}|y|^{1/2}+F(y, 0, x, t)t^{\frac{1}{3} - \delta} - \frac{1}{2}c(\gamma,t)|x|^{1/2}\right\} - \frac{1}{2}c_{\gamma,t}|x|^{1/2}.
\end{align*}

Now, since $F(y, 0, x, t) \leq \mathcal{C}(1+|x|^{1/5}+|y|^{1/5} + |t|^{1/5})$, it is easy to see that the first term in the previous displayed inequality is an almost surely finite random constant that depends on only $\gamma$ and $T$; we label it $\mathcal{B}$. Boundedness and decay at infinity of the KPZ fixed point follow readily from \eqref{eq:KPZ_is_bounded}.

nodes.statement: We make use of Lemma~ which implies that, for delta in (0,1/2], 0< T_0 leq T, and L>0, there exists a random constant mathcal C_L (depending also on delta, T_0, and T) such that, for all sin[T_0,T] and x, y, and z with |x|, |y|, |z| leq L, |mathcal L(z,0; y, s) - mathcal L(z, 0; x, s)| leq mathcal C_L|x-y|^frac12-delta. Now we observe that, for any x,yinR, h_s(y) - h_s(x) &= sup_zinR left(h_0(z) + mathcal L(z,0;y,s)right) - sup_zinRleft(h_0(z) + mathcal L(z,0;x,s)right)\\ &leq mathcal L(z_s^*(y), 0; y,s) - mathcal L(z_s^*(y), 0; x,s), where z_s^*(y) is the element of minimum absolute value in the set of maximizers of the first supremum. Define bar z = sup_sin[T_0, T]sup_|y|leq K |z_s^*(y)|. We claim that bar z is almost surely finite. Before proving the claim, we show how it completes the proof of Lemma~. Since delta, T_0, and T are fixed, let, for LinN, mathcal C_L be the corresponding constant in . Define mathcal C by setting it to be mathcal C_L on the event that bar zin [L, L+1], for every Lgeq lceil K rceil, and to be mathcal C_lceil Krceil on the event that bar z in [0, lceil Krceil]. Then we have that h_s(y) -h_s(x) leq mathcal C|x-y|^1/2-delta for all |x|,|y| leq K and sin [T_0,T]; by symmetry, the same upper bound holds for |h_s(y) - h_s(x)|. Since mathcal C is clearly almost surely finite, Lemma~ follows conditional upon the claim. We now prove the claim that bar z <infty almost surely. Let z_0inR be such that h_0(z_0) > -infty. It is enough to prove that h_0(z_0) + inf_sin[T_0,T]inf_|y|leq K mathcal L(z_0,0;y,s) =: -R > -infty, i.e., R<infty, and that there exists a random constant M depending on only T_0, T, and K such that sup_|z| geq M (h_0(z)+mathcal L(z,0;y,s)) < -R for all |y|leq K. That R<infty follows immediately from the continuity of mathcal L and the definition of z_0. To find the random M satisfying the conditions, we observe that, from Assumption~ and with delta=1/3, h_0(z)+mathcal L(z,0;y,s) &leq alpha-gamma |z|^1/2 + F_1/3(z,0,y,s) - frac(z-y)^2s\\ &leq alpha-gamma |z|^1/2 + F_1/3(z,0,K,T) - frac(z-y)^2T_0. It is easy to see that we can find M large enough depending on only alpha, gamma, K, T and T_0 such that |z| > M implies that the previous expression is smaller than -R for all y with |y|leq K. This completes the proof of the claim, and thus of Lemma~.

nodes.statement: For s < t, the variational formula yields h_t(x) - h_s(x) = sup_y in R bigl\ h_s(y) - h_s(x) + L(y, s; x, t) bigr\. We wish to bound h_s(y) -h_s(x) by mathcal C|y-x|^1/2-delta for a random constant mathcal C uniform in sin[T_0,T] using Lemma~. However, this requires that y be restricted to a compact interval, and so we start by showing that we may localize the supremum in the previous display to a compact interval. More precisely, letting y_s,t^*(x) be the maximizer of the supremum in of minimum absolute value, we claim that, almost surely, sup_|x|leq Lsup_sneq tin[T_0, T] |y_s,t^*(x)| < infty. First let R' = -inf_|x|leq Linf_sin[T_0,T] h_s(x). By the variational formula and the continuity of L, we have that R'<infty almost surely. Thus we see that sup_y in R bigl\ h_s(y) + L(y, s; x, t) bigr\ geq h_s(x) + L(x,s; x,t) geq -R' + inf_|x|leq Linf_sneq tin[T_0,T] L(x,s; x,t) =: -R. Bounds on L imply that R<infty almost surely; note that, by definition, R is uniform over |x|leq L and s,tin[T_0,T]. Thus, to prove , it is enough to show that there exists a random M large enough such that, for all sneq tin[T_0,T] and |x|leq L, sup_|y|geq M bigl\h_s(y) + L(y,s; x,t) bigr\ < -R. As in the proof of Lemma~, this follows by using that L(y,s; x,t) leq F_1/3(y,s,x,t) - frac(x-y)^2t-s and a uniform decay estimate on h_s(y). This decay estimate, provided by Lemma~, asserts that h_s(y) leq B - frac18min(t^-1, sqrt2gamma) |y|^1/2 leq B - frac18min(T^-1, sqrt2gamma) |y|^1/2 for all s,tin[T_0, T] and yin R, where B is uniform over sin[T_0,T]. Thus, using the random M which satisfies above, we see that may be written as h_t(x) - h_s(x) = sup_|y| leq M bigl\ h_s(y) - h_s(x) + L(y, s; x, t) bigr\. Now, from Lemma~, for given delta_1>0, there exists a random constant mathcal C_1 such that, for all x,y in[-M,M] and sin[T_0,T], |h_s(y) - h_s(x)| leq mathcal C_1|y-x|^frac12-delta_1; though M is random, we know such a random and a.s. finite constant mathcal C_1 exists by applying Lemma~ on each of the events Min[m,m+1] for minN and getting a different random constant on eachof these disjoint events. Applying this and bounds on mathcal L from in yields, for |x|leq L and s,t in[T_0,T], h_t(x)-h_s(x) &leq sup_|y|leq M left\mathcal C_1|y-x|^frac12-delta_1 + F_delta(y,s,x,t)|t-s|^frac13-delta - frac(x-y)^2t-sright\ \\ &leq sup_|y|leq M left\mathcal C_1|y-x|^frac12-delta_1 - frac(x-y)^2t-sright\ + F_delta(M,T,L,T)|t-s|^frac13-delta. Simple calculus yields that the supremum is at most mathcal C_2 |t-s|^1/3-delta_2 for a random constant mathcal C_2, where delta_2 = 8delta_1/(9+6delta_1). We set delta_1 so that delta_2 equals the given positive value delta in Lemma~, thus obtaining h_t(x)-h_s(x) leq mathcal C_3 |t-s|^1/3-delta for a random constant mathcal C_3 and for all |x|leq L and s,tin[T_0,T]. For the lower bound, again and imply h_t(x)-h_s(x) &geq sup_|y|leq M left\-mathcal C_1|y-x|^frac12-delta - F_delta(y,s,x,t)|t-s|^frac13-delta - frac(x-y)^2t-sright\,\\ &geq -mathcal C_4 |t-s|^frac13-delta, by noting that F_delta(y,s,x,t) leq F_delta(M,T,L,T) and considering the value of the remaining expression at y = x, which satisfies |y| leq M by assuming M>L if necessary. This completes the proof of Lemma~.

nodes.statement: We recall our notation eta_i = (varepsilon_i, delta_i) geq 0, and throughout the proof we consider values varepsilon_i, delta_i in (0,fracA2]. This, in particular, implies that the two intervals in the definition do not intersect. We start by proving existence of the limit and the formula . Definitions , and the definition in of the function g_eta_1, eta_2 yield MoveEqLeft[7] fracBigl(Q_L^(eta_1; eta_2) - Q_L^(eta_1; 0)Bigr)(u_1, u_2)p_2 L(u_2 - u_1)\\ &=mathbb P_B(-L)=u_1, B(L)=u_2Bigl(B(y)>-g_eta_1, eta_2(y) for y in [-L,L]Bigr) \\ & - mathbb P_B(-L)=u_1, B(L)=u_2Bigl(B(y)>-g_eta_1, 0(y) for y in [-L,L]Bigr)\\ &= - mathbb P_B(-L)=u_1, B(L)=u_2Bigl(B(y)>-g_eta_1, 0(y) for y in [-L,L],\, \\ & hspace2cm B(z) in (-M, -M + varepsilon_2] for some z in [x_2, x_2 + delta_2)Bigr), where B is a Brownian bridge with variance two. It will be convenient to view the Brownian bridge B going from the point u_2 at time L to the point u_1 at time -L. Let us then define the hitting time tau^(a) := sup \z leq x_2 + delta_2: B(z) = a\. Then formula can be written as MoveEqLeft[6] fracBigl(Q_L^(eta_1; eta_2) - Q_L^(eta_1; 0)Bigr)(u_1, u_2)p_2 L(u_2 - u_1)\\ &= - mathbb P_B(-L)=u_1, B(L)=u_2Bigl(B(y)>-g_eta_1, 0(y) for y in [-L,L],\, \\ & hspace6cm tau^(-M + varepsilon_2) in [x_2, x_2 + delta_2)Bigr). We note that if the value of the Brownian motion B(x_2 + delta_2) is in (-M, -M + varepsilon_2), then hitting of the box [x_2, x_2 + delta_2) times (-M, -M + varepsilon_2] happens at time x_2 + delta_2 (this is due to continuity of Brownian motion). Since we excluded the point x_2 + delta_2 in , hitting can happen only at the level -M + varepsilon_2 on the time interval [x_2, x_2 + delta_2). Moreover, if the value of B(x_2 + delta_2) is in [-M + varepsilon_2, infty), then hitting of the box happens almost surely at tau^(-M + varepsilon_2) in [x_2, x_2 + delta_2). [h] includegraphics[width=textwidth]Qform-new.pdf captionsetupwidth=.9linewidth captionAn illustration of . The Brownian motion B starts at height u_2 at time L and runs backwards in time until height v at time x_2+delta_2, conditioned to avoid the solid line at height -M all the while. From height v, the path runs until a time z with sub-probability measure F^(-M + varepsilon_2)_[z, delta_2] (v)dz on the interval zin [x_2,x_2+delta). This point is the time when the Brownian motion hits height -M+varepsilon_2, provided it occurs in the time interval [x_2,x_2+delta_2). nodes.statement: We may write the probability on the left-hand side of for the cut-off as mathbb P_h_0 Bigl(h^L_t in TPA, bar L^varepsilonBigr) = sum_M in varepsilon Z mathbb P_h_0 Bigl(h^L_t in TPA, bar L^varepsilon,\, Max(h^L_t) in (M-varepsilon, M]Bigr). Let us define the varepsilon-fattening of J_bar L by J_bar L^varepsilon := bigcup_x in J_bar L [x - varepsilon, x + varepsilon]. From the definition of the set TPA, bar L^varepsilon, we conclude that, if J_bar L^1/2^varepsilon cap (M-varepsilon, M] = varnothing, then the term indexed by M in the sum vanishes. When this term does not vanish, we can estimate it by &mathbb P_h_0 Bigl(h^L_t in TPA, bar L^varepsilon,\, Max(h^L_t) in (M-varepsilon, M]Bigr) \\ & leq mathbb P_h_0 Bigl(exists\, x_1, x_2 in J_L : x_2 - x_1 geq A,\; h_t(x_i) > M - 2 varepsilon,\; h_t(y) leq M ~for~ y in [- L, L]Bigr). For 0 < delta leq A, denote overline eta = (2 varepsilon, delta), and let A_delta be the largest value in delta Z such that 0 < A_delta leq A. Then, using the function F_t, M, L^(eta_1; eta_2)(x_1, x_2), defined in , we have the upper bound mathbb P_h_0 Bigl(h^L_t in TPA, bar L^varepsilonBigr) leq sum_substackx_1, x_2 in (delta Z) cap J_ L^delta \\ x_2 - x_1 geq A_delta sum_M in (varepsilon Z) cap J_bar L^1/2^varepsilon F^(overlineeta; overlineeta)_t, M, L(x_1, x_2). For 0 < delta_1 leq delta_2 and 0 < varepsilon_1 leq varepsilon_2, let us set overline eta_1 = (2 varepsilon_1, delta_1) and overline eta_2 = (2 varepsilon_2, delta_2). Moreover, we define I^(overlineeta_1; overlineeta_2) := sum_substackx_1, x_2 in (delta_1 Z) cap J_ L^delta_1 \\ x_2 - x_1 geq A_delta_1 sum_M in (varepsilon_1 Z) cap J_bar L^1/2^varepsilon_1 F^(overlineeta_1; overlineeta_2)_t, M, L(x_1, x_2), where we prefer to suppress dependence on the variables t, A, etc. Then reads as mathbb P_h_0 Bigl(h^L_t in TPA, bar L^varepsilonBigr) leq I^(overlineeta; overlineeta). From , we conclude that for every fixed bar eta_1 > 0 the following limit holds: mylimbar eta_2 searrow 0 frac1|bar eta_2| I^(bar eta_1; bar eta_2) = sum_substackx_1, x_2 in (delta_1 Z) cap J_ L^delta_1 \\ x_2 - x_1 geq A_delta_1 sum_M in (varepsilon_1 Z) cap J_bar L^1/2^varepsilon_1 F^(overlineeta_1; star)_t, M, L(x_1, x_2)=:I^(bar eta_1; star). Since the limit holds uniformly over eta_1 and since the function F^(overlineeta; overlineeta)_t, M, L(x_1, x_2) is positive, we conclude that there exist constants chi_1 > 0 and C_1 > 0, independent of bar eta_1 and bar eta_2, such that I^(bar eta_1; bar eta_2) leq C_1 |bar eta_2|\, I^(bar eta_1; star), for all bar eta_1, bar eta_2 in (0, chi_1]^2 and bar eta_2 in Dom (this domain is defined in ). Now we claim that mylimbar eta_1 searrow 0 varepsilon_1^-1 |bar eta_1| I^(bar eta_1; star) = C_2 int_-beta L^beta L - A d x_1 int_x_1 + A^beta L d x_2 int_-beta sqrtbar L^beta sqrtbar L d M\; F_t, M, L(x_1, x_2)=:I, for a constant C_2 > 0 which we define later, and where the constant beta arises from the definition of J_ L. We note that continuity of the function F_t, M, L, proved in Proposition~, guarantees that the latter triple integral is well-defined. We postpone our proof of this limit for the moment, and show how it implies the bound . From , we conclude that there exist constants chi_3 > 0 and C_3 > 0 such that I^(bar eta_1; star) leq C_3 fracvarepsilon_1|bar eta_1| I, for all bar eta_1 in (0,chi_3]^2 cap Dom. nodes.statement: Set y_n(x) equal to arg\,max_y left(h_0(y) + S_n(y,x)right) (taking the choice of largest absolute value when it is not unique). Fix M>0. We claim that (y_n(x))_ninN is uniformly tight for xin[-M,M]. To show this, let varepsilon>0 be given and let Rgeq Mvee theta, so that we may choose y_0 in[0,R] such that h_0(y_0) geq -2theta. Then we observe that, for every K>0, MoveEqLeft mathbb Pbig(y_n(x) > Rbig) \\ &leq mathbb Pleft(sup_Rleq y leq n^1/60 big(h_0(y) + S_n(y,x)big) > h_0(y_0) + S_n(y_0,x)right)\\ &leq mathbb Pleft(sup_Rleq y leq n^1/60 big(h_0(y) + S_n(y,x)big) > -Kright) + mathbb PBig(h_0(y_0) + S_n(y_0,x) < -KBig). We set K geq 4theta large enough that h_0(y_0) geq -2theta geq -K/2 and K geq (y_0-x)^2 (for example by setting Kgeq 4R^2). Then we bound the second term of by CR^2exp(-cK^3/2) (uniformly for all xin[-M,M]) by Proposition~. Thus, for all K large enough, the second term is at most varepsilon/2. Next we bound the first term of . By a union bound, mathbb Pleft(sup_Rleq y leq n^1/60 big(h_0(y) + S_n(y,x)big) > -Kright) &leq sum_j=R^lceil n^1/60rceil mathbb Pleft(sup_y in [j,j+1] big(S_n(y,x) - gamma |y|^1/2big) > -Kright)\\ &leq sum_j=R^lceil n^1/60rceil mathbb Pleft(sup_y in [j,j+1] S_n(y,x) > -K + gamma j^1/2right). Setting R such that gamma j^1/2 > 2K for all jgeq R shows that each summand in the last display is bounded above by Cj^2 exp(-c j^3/4), uniformly over xin[-M,M], again by Proposition~. nodes.name: Proof of Lemma~\ref{l.P_n Brownian gibbs}
nodes.statement: As mentioned, this follows from P_n being an affine transformation of n-level Dyson Brownian motion (Lemma~) and the latter ensemble having the Brownian Gibbs property. We briefly outline how to show that n-level Dyson Brownian motion DBM_n : intintntimes[0,infty)toR has this property. Let [a,b] subseteq (0,infty). We first condition on the sigma-algebra generated by \DBM_n,j(x) : jinllbracket 1,nrrbracket, x in [0, infty)setminus [a,b]\. The Markov property of DBM_n then implies that this conditional distribution depends on only the boundary values \DBM_n,j(x) : jinintintn, xin\a,b\\. Then the conditional distribution is that of n non-intersecting Brownian bridges with the given endpoints, as can be verified by comparing the transition probabilities of this ensemble (which makes use of the Karlin-McGregor formula for non-intersecting strong Markov processes) with that of the conditioned Dyson Brownian motion (see, for example, for the transition probability formulas of Dyson Brownian motion). The ensemble of non-intersecting Brownian bridges, quite naturally, has the Brownian Gibbs property .

As mentioned, this follows from $\mathcal{P}_n$ being an affine transformation of $n$-level Dyson Brownian motion (Lemma~\ref{l.dyson brownian motion}) and the latter ensemble having the Brownian Gibbs property. We briefly outline how to show that $n$-level Dyson Brownian motion $\mathrm{DBM}_n : \intint{n}\times[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}$ has this property.

Let $[a,b] \subseteq (0,\infty)$. We first condition on the $\sigma$-algebra generated by $\{\mathrm{DBM}_{n,j}(x) : j\in\llbracket 1,n\rrbracket, x \in [0, \infty)\setminus [a,b]\}$. The Markov property of $\mathrm{DBM}_n$ then implies that this conditional distribution depends on only the boundary values $\{\mathrm{DBM}_{n,j}(x) : j\in\intint{n}, x\in\{a,b\}\}$. Then the conditional distribution is that of $n$ non-intersecting Brownian bridges with the given endpoints, as can be verified by comparing the transition probabilities of this ensemble (which makes use of the Karlin-McGregor formula \cite{karlinMcGregor} for non-intersecting strong Markov processes) with that of the conditioned Dyson Brownian motion (see, for example, \cite[Section~3]{warren2007dyson} for the transition probability formulas of Dyson Brownian motion). The ensemble of non-intersecting Brownian bridges, quite naturally, has the Brownian Gibbs property \cite[Lemma 2.13]{dimitrov2020characterization}.

For convenience of notation, let us define

$$h(z) = \sup_{x\in[x_0+A,x_0+A+ 2]}\hz{z}(x).$$

The arguments that we will present hold on the probability one event $\Omega$ that, for each $z\in \mathbb{R}$, there exist $x\in [x_0+A,x_0+A+ 2]$, $y\in [0, n^{1/60}]$ and an upright path $\Gamma^{z,x}$ (for which we use the capital Greek letter to emphasise the path's randomness) ending at $x$, such that

$$h(z) = \mathfrak{h}_0(y) + \mathcal{P}_n^z[\Gamma^{z,x}] - n^{2/3};$$

that the supremum in the definition of $h$ is achieved uses the compactness of $[x_0+A,x_0+A+ 2]$.

By symmetry, it is enough to prove that $h(z_1) - h(z_2) \leq 2 |z_1-z_2|.$
On the event $\Omega$, we see that, for some $y\in [0, n^{1/60}]$, $x\in [x_0+A,x_0+A+ 2]$, and upright path $\Gamma^{z_1,x}$,

\begin{align*}
h(z_1) &= \mathfrak{h}_0(y) + \mathcal{P}^{z_1}_n[\Gamma^{z_1,x}] - n^{2/3},\\
h(z_2) &\geq \mathfrak{h}_0(y) + \mathcal{P}^{z_2}_n[\Gamma^{z_1,x}] - n^{2/3},
\end{align*}

and so

$$h(z_1) - h(z_2) \leq \mathcal{P}_n^{z_1}[\Gamma^{z_1,x}] - \mathcal{P}_n^{z_2}[\Gamma^{z_1,x}].$$

Let $u$ be the coordinate where $\Gamma^{z_1,x}$ jumps to the top line. Since the environments defined by $\mathcal{P}_n^{z_1}$ and $\mathcal{P}_n^{z_2}$ differ only in the top line, we see that

\begin{align*}
\mathcal{P}_n^{z_1}[\Gamma^{z_1,x}] - \mathcal{P}_n^{z_2}[\Gamma^{z_1,x}]

&=\big[\mathcal{P}_{n,1}^{z_1}(x) - \mathcal{P}_{n,1}^{z_1}(u)\big] - \big[\mathcal{P}_{n,1}^{z_2}(x) - \mathcal{P}_{n,1}^{z_2}(u)\big] \\

&= \big[\mathcal{P}_{n,1}^{z_1}(x) - \mathcal{P}_{n,1}^{z_2}(x)\big] - \big[\mathcal{P}_{n,1}^{z_1}(u) - \mathcal{P}_{n,1}^{z_2}(u)\big]\\

&\leq 2|z_1-z_2|.
\end{align*}

The inequality follows from the definition of $\mathcal{P}^z_{n,1}$ in \eqref{e.L^z formula}.
The equalities and the bound hold deterministically  on $\Omega$. This completes the proof of Lemma~\ref{l.lipschitz}.

nodes.statement: First we recall that x_0geq -n^1/60 by definition and so F^past_-n^1/60subseteq F^past_x_0. Conditional on F_lower, F^past_-n^1/60 and F^future_n^1/60, the distribution of \P_n,1(x) : -n^1/60 leq x leq n^1/60\ is that of a Brownian bridge of rate two on [-n^1/60,n^1/60] with starting value P_n,1(-n^1/60) and ending value P_n,1(n^1/60) conditioned on non-intersection with the second curve P_n,2(mathpalettemathpalettemathpalettemathpalettemathpalettemathpalettemathpalettemathpalettebigcdot@.5@.5@.5@.5@.5@.5@.5@.5). This is the statement of the Brownian Gibbs property of P_n, Lemma~. In particular, the conditioned process is Markov (and non-homogeneous), and, since Brownian bridge is a strong Markov process and the conditioning event is almost surely of positive probability, the same is true of the conditioned space-time process. (Here we consider the space-time process so as to have a time-homogeneous Markov process: see .) Consider the process X : [-n^1/60, infty)to [-infty,infty]^2times[-n^1/60,infty] defined by X(t) := (P_n,1(twedge n^1/60), h^scriptscriptstyle(nscriptscriptstyle)(twedge n^1/60), t); here [-infty,infty] and [-n^1/60,infty] are compactifications of R and [-n^1/60,infty), and are employed so that the state space of X is compact. We consider X to start at time -n^1/60, and to be killed at time n^1/60, so that the maximizer of the second component of X is x_0^n = arg\,max_|x|leq n^1/60 h^scriptscriptstyle(nscriptscriptstyle)(x). (To be precise, as earlier we will be working with the final maximizer, i.e., the largest one, on the event that there are several. To see that there is such a final maximizer for the process h^scriptscriptstyle(nscriptscriptstyle)(twedge n^1/60), note that there must be a final one on the interval [-n^1/60, n^1/60] by continuity of h^scriptscriptstyle(nscriptscriptstyle), and that, by Lemma~ ahead, the final one is almost surely not n^1/60.) We claim that, conditionally on F_lower, F^past_-n^1/60 and F^future_n^1/60, X is a homogeneous strong Markov process. To see this, first define the process X' by X'(t) = big( P_n,1(twedge n^1/60), h^scriptscriptstyle(nscriptscriptstyle)(t wedge n^1/60) big). It is enough to prove that X' is a non-homogeneous Markov process, as then, by the same trick as used a few lines above, the space-time process X(t) = (X'(t), t) is necessarily a homogeneous Markov process. To show that X' is Markov under this conditioning, we state a formula that expresses h^scriptscriptstyle(nscriptscriptstyle)(t+s) in terms of h^scriptscriptstyle(nscriptscriptstyle)(t) and data contained in F_lower, F^past_-n^1/60 and F^future_n^1/60: h^scriptscriptstyle(nscriptscriptstyle)(t+s) &= maxbigg\h^scriptscriptstyle(nscriptscriptstyle)(t) + P_n,1(t+s) - P_n,1(t),\\ &hspace-0.3cm sup_substacky\\ u> tBig(h_0(y) + P_n[(-tfrac12n^1/3+y, n)to (u,2)] + P_n,1(t+s) - P_n,1(u) - n^2/3Big)bigg\; the supremum over y and u is taken over choices such that 0leq yleq n^1/60 and yleq -frac12n^1/3+~u. This formula follows by considering the location u that the geodesic for endpoint t+s jumps to the top line. It is the first term that attains the maximum when uleq t; and it is the second that does so when u>t. In the first case, h^scriptscriptstyle(nscriptscriptstyle)(t+s) is equal to h^scriptscriptstyle(nscriptscriptstyle)(t) plus the remaining increment on the top line as the (t+s)-geodesic must pass through (t,1); this is because h^scriptscriptstyle(nscriptscriptstyle)(t) is the value attained by a similar maximization problem. We start by specifying some further good events. Let $y_0\in[-\theta,\theta]$ be some fixed real number such that  $\mathfrak{h}_0(y_0) \geq -2\theta$. For $M>0$ to be specified later, define

\begin{align*}
\mathsf F_3 &= \bigl\{|\mathfrak{h}^{{\scriptscriptstyle(}n{\scriptscriptstyle)}}(x_0)| \leq K\bigr\}, \qquad &\mathsf F_4 &= \big\{|x_0| \leq M\big\},\\ \qquad 

\mathsf F_5 &= \Big\{\mathcal{S}_n(y_0, -M) \geq -K/2\Big\}, \qquad &\mathsf F_6 &= \Big\{\mathcal{P}_{n,1}(-M) \leq K/2\Big\}.
\end{align*}

Note that $\mathsf{Fav}_{K, L}\supseteq \mathsf F_1\cap\mathsf F_2\cap\mathsf F_3\cap \mathsf F_4$ when $\beta L\geq M+A+2$ and $\beta L^{1/2}\geq K$. We set $L_0$ high enough that both conditions on $L$ are met whenever $L\geq L_0$ (when $K$ and $M$ are set, which will be done in a way not depending on $L$).

We will show that $\mathbb P\left(\mathsf{Fav}_{K, L}^c\right) \leq \tfrac{1}{2}$ for large enough $K$ and $L$ by showing the stronger statement that, for $\delta=1/10$ and appropriate choices of $K$, $L$, and $M$, we have

$$\mathbb P\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^6 \mathsf F_i^c\right) \leq 5\delta = \frac{1}{2}.$$


\noindent\emph{Bounding $\mathbb P(\mathsf F_4^c)$}: This is a simple application of Lemma~\ref{l.tightness of prelimiting maximizer}, which yields $M = M(\gamma,\theta)$ such that $\mathbb P(\mathsf F_4^c) \leq \delta = \frac{1}{10}$ for $n\geq n_0 = n_0(\gamma,\theta)$. We fix the value of $M$ obtained here for the rest of the proof.
\medskip


\noindent\emph{Bounding $\mathbb P(\mathsf F_2^c\cap \mathsf F_4)$}: On the event $\mathsf F_4$ we have $|x_0|\leq M$. Also, for large enough $K$ depending only on $\delta=1/10$, $A$, and $M$,

$$\mathbb P\left(\inf_{|x|\leq M+A+2} \mathcal{P}_{n,1}(x) < -K\right) \leq \delta/2 \quad\text{and}\quad \mathbb P\left(\sup_{|x| \leq M+A+2} \mathcal{P}_{n,1}(x) > K\right) \leq \delta/2;$$

this is implied by Proposition~\ref{l.BrLPP uniform tail bound} after recalling from \eqref{e.P S identity} that $\mathcal{P}_{n,1}(x) = \mathcal{S}_n(0, x)$.
Thus $\mathbb P(\mathsf F_2^c\cap \mathsf F_4)$ is at most $\delta$, since $\mu = \frac{1}{2}(\mathcal{P}_{n,1}(x_0+ A) + \mathcal{P}_{n,1}(x_0+A+2))$ is bounded above and below on $\mathsf F_4$ by $\sup_{x\in[-M-A-2, M+A+2]} \mathcal{P}_{n,1}(x)$ and $\inf_{x\in[-M-A-2, M+A+2]} \mathcal{P}_{n,1}(x)$.
\medskip

\noindent\emph{Bounding $\mathbb P(\mathsf F_5^c)$ and $\mathbb P(\mathsf F_6^c)$}: These correspond respectively to lower and upper tails on one-point last passage values, i.e., on $\mathcal{S}_n(y,x)$ for fixed $y$ and $x$, because $\mathcal{P}_{n,1}(-M) = \mathcal{S}_n(0, -M)$ in view of \eqref{e.P S identity}. Thus, we obtain $\mathbb P(\mathsf F_5^c) \leq \delta$ and $\mathbb P(\mathsf F_6^c) \leq \delta$ by applying Proposition~\ref{l.BrLPP uniform tail bound} in a closed interval of unit length around the starting and ending points and by setting $K$ high enough, depending on $\theta$.
\medskip

\noindent\emph{Bounding $\mathbb P(\mathsf F_3^c\cap \mathsf F_4 \cap \mathsf F_5)$}: We first bound the probability that $\mathfrak{h}^{{\scriptscriptstyle(}n{\scriptscriptstyle)}}(x_0) \geq K$ on $\mathsf F_4$. Recall that, by assumption, $ \mathfrak{h}_0(y) \leq - \gamma |y|^{1/2}$ for all $y\in \mathbb{R}$. 
Note that, on $\mathsf F_4$,

$\mathfrak{h}^{{\scriptscriptstyle(}n{\scriptscriptstyle)}}(x_0) = \sup_{|x|\leq M} \mathfrak{h}^{{\scriptscriptstyle(}n{\scriptscriptstyle)}}(x).$

Thus,

\begin{align*}
\sup_{|x|\leq M}\mathfrak{h}^{{\scriptscriptstyle(}n{\scriptscriptstyle)}}(x)

= \sup_{\substack{|x|\leq M\\ 0\leq y \leq n^{1/60}}}\Big(\mathfrak{h}_0(y) + \mathcal{S}_n(y, x)\Big)

&\leq \sup_{\substack{|x|\leq M\\ 0\leq y \leq n^{1/60}}} \left(\mathcal{S}_n(y,x) - \gamma |y|^{1/2}\right).
\end{align*}

By a union bound, we can bound $\mathbb P\left(\sup_{|x|\leq M} \mathfrak{h}^{{\scriptscriptstyle(}n{\scriptscriptstyle)}}(x) > K\right)$ above by

\begin{align*}
\sum_{j=0}^{\lceil n^{1/60}\rceil } \mathbb P\Bigg(\sup_{\substack{|x|\leq M\\ y \in[j,j+1]}} \left(\mathcal{S}_n(y,x) - \gamma |y|^{1/2}\right) > K\Bigg) 

&\leq \sum_{j=0}^{\lceil n^{1/60}\rceil } \mathbb P\Bigg(\sup_{\substack{|x|\leq M\\ y \in[j,j+1]}} \mathcal{S}_n(y,x) > K + \gamma j^{1/2}\Bigg)\\

&\leq \sum_{j=0}^{\lceil n^{1/60}\rceil } C\max(M^2, j^2) \exp\left(-c(K^{3/2} + j^{3/4})\right),
\end{align*}

the final inequality by an application of Proposition~\ref{l.BrLPP uniform tail bound}. The final expression can be made less than $\delta=\frac{1}{10}$ by raising $K$ appropriately (depending on $M$ and $\gamma$) if needed. Doing so, we learn that $\mathbb P(\{\mathfrak{h}^{{\scriptscriptstyle(}n{\scriptscriptstyle)}}(x_0)\geq K\}\cap \mathsf F_4) \leq \delta$.

Next we bound the probability that $\mathfrak{h}^{{\scriptscriptstyle(}n{\scriptscriptstyle)}}(x_0) \leq -K$ on $\mathsf F_5$.  Recall that $y_0\in [-\theta,\theta]$ is such that $\mathfrak{h}_0(y_0) \geq -2\theta$, and increase $K$ if needed so that $\mathfrak{h}_0(y_0) \geq -K/3$. Since $x_0$ is the maximizer of $\mathfrak{h}^{{\scriptscriptstyle(}n{\scriptscriptstyle)}}$, and  \eqref{e.prelimiting gen profile formula} holds, we see that

$$\mathfrak{h}^{{\scriptscriptstyle(}n{\scriptscriptstyle)}}(x_0) \geq \mathfrak{h}_0(y_0) + \mathcal{S}_n(y_0, -M) \geq -5K/6 > -K,$$

the last inequality holding on $F_5$. Thus $\mathbb P(\{\mathfrak{h}^{{\scriptscriptstyle(}n{\scriptscriptstyle)}}(x_0) \leq -K\}\cap F_5) = 0$. Overall we have shown that $\mathbb P(\mathsf F_3^c \cap \mathsf F_4\cap \mathsf F_5) \leq \delta$.

\medskip


\noindent\emph{Bounding $\mathbb P(\mathsf F_1^c\cap \mathsf F_3\cap \mathsf F_4\cap \mathsf F_5\cap \mathsf F_6)$}: Recall that we have set $y_0$ and $K$ such that $\mathfrak{h}_0(y_0) \geq -K/3 > -K$. Observe that $\smash{\mathrm{Corner}^{\uparrow}} > 4K$ implies that there is a value of $z$ in $[4K, \infty)$ such that $\mathfrak{h}^{{\scriptscriptstyle(}n{\scriptscriptstyle)}}(x_0) = \sup_{x\in [x_0+A,x_0+A+2]} \hz{z}(x)$ by Lemma~\ref{l.conditional distribution}. But we will now show that if $z\geq 4K$, then, on the event $\bigcap_{i=3}^6 \mathsf F_i$, we have that $\hz{z}(x_0+A+1) > \mathfrak{h}^{{\scriptscriptstyle(}n{\scriptscriptstyle)}}(x_0)$; this is a contradiction and so the probability we are bounding must be zero.
We use the formula for $\hz{z}$ from \eqref{e.L^f representation}, and the formula \eqref{e.melon LPP and S_n} relating $\mathcal{S}_n$ and LPP values through $\mathcal{P}_n$. Indeed, if $z\geq 4K$ and the event $\bigcap_{i=3}^6 \mathsf F_i$ holds, then

\begin{align*}
\hz{z}(x_0+A+1) &= \sup_{0\leq y \leq n^{1/60}} \Big(\mathfrak{h}_0(y) + \mathcal{P}_n^{z}[(-\tfrac12n^{1/3}+ y, n) \to (x_0+A+1, 1)]-n^{2/3}\Big)\\

&\geq -K + \left(\mathcal{P}_n^z[(-\tfrac12n^{1/3}+ y_0, n) \to (-M, 1)] - n^{2/3}\right)\\

&\quad + \mathcal{P}_n^z[(-M, 1) \to (x_0+A+1,1)]\\

&= -K + \mathcal{S}_n(y_0, -M) + z - \mathcal{P}_{n,1}(-M)\\

&\geq 3K + \mathcal{S}_n(y_0, -M)  - \mathcal{P}_{n,1}(-M) \geq 2K.
\end{align*}

The first inequality bounded the supremum by the choice of $y=y_0$ and used our assumption that $\mathfrak{h}_0(y_0) > -K$; the penultimate inequality used the assumption that $z\geq4K$;  and the final inequality used the bounds that hold on $\mathsf F_5\cap\mathsf F_6$.


The conclusion $\hz{z}(x_0+A+1)  \geq 2K$ contradicts $\mathfrak{h}^{{\scriptscriptstyle(}n{\scriptscriptstyle)}}(x_0) \leq K$, which holds on $\mathsf F_4$, since, on this event, $x_0+A+1 \in [-M,M]$. Thus the probability we are bounding is zero.

Overall we have shown that $\mathbb P\big(\bigcup_{i=1}^6 \mathsf F_i^c\big) \leq 5\delta = 1/2$. It may be easily checked that the setting of $K$ and $L_0$ can be made to depend on $\gamma$, $\theta$, and $A$ continuously, completing the proof of Lemma~\ref{l.fav probability}.

We fix $K$ and $L_0$ as given by Lemma~\ref{l.fav probability}. For any given $L>L_0$, we have that $\mathbb P(\mathsf{Fav}_{K,L}) \geq 1/2$.

Recall $x_0  = x_0^{n}= arg\,max_{|x|\leq n^{1/60}} \mathfrak{h}^{{\scriptscriptstyle(}n{\scriptscriptstyle)}}(x)$. We have that

\begin{align*}
\MoveEqLeft
\mathbb P\left(\sup_{x\in [x_0+A,x_0+A+2]} \mathfrak{h}^{{\scriptscriptstyle(}n{\scriptscriptstyle)}}(x) > \mathfrak{h}^{{\scriptscriptstyle(}n{\scriptscriptstyle)}}(x_0) - \varepsilon;\, |\mathfrak{h}^{{\scriptscriptstyle(}n{\scriptscriptstyle)}}(x_0)| \leq \beta L^{1/2};\, |x_0|\leq \beta L-A-2\right)\\

&\hspace{-0.3cm}= \mathbb E\left[\mathbb P\left(\sup_{x\in [x_0+A,x_0+A+2]} \mathfrak{h}^{{\scriptscriptstyle(}n{\scriptscriptstyle)}}(x) > \mathfrak{h}^{{\scriptscriptstyle(}n{\scriptscriptstyle)}}(x_0) - \varepsilon \ \bigg|\ \mathscr{F}\right)\mathbbm{1}_{|\mathfrak{h}^{{\scriptscriptstyle(}n{\scriptscriptstyle)}}(x_0)| \leq \beta L^{1/2}\, |x_0|\leq \beta L-A-2}\right].
\end{align*}

We have to bound below the inner conditional probability. Set $\mathsf{Fav} = \mathsf{Fav}_{K,L}$ for notational convenience. Recall that the occurrence of $\mathsf{Fav}$ implies that $|x_0|\leq \beta L-A-2$ and $|\mathfrak{h}^{{\scriptscriptstyle(}n{\scriptscriptstyle)}}(x_0)| \leq \beta L^{1/2}$. We claim that, on $\mathsf{Fav}$, the event of the inner conditional probability is implied by

\begin{equation}\label{e.I_epsilon}
Z := \mathcal{P}_{n,1}(x_0+A+1) \in \left[\mathrm{Corner}^{\downarrow}\vee (\mathrm{Corner}^{\uparrow}-\varepsilon/2),\  \mathrm{Corner}^{\uparrow}\right]=:I_{\varepsilon}.
\end{equation}

The validity of the claim follows from two facts. The first is that $\sup_{x\in [x_0+A,x_0+A+2]} \hz{z}(x) = \mathfrak{h}^{{\scriptscriptstyle(}n{\scriptscriptstyle)}}(x_0)$ when $z=\mathrm{Corner}^{\uparrow}$ (from Lemma~\ref{l.conditional distribution}); and the second is that,  almost surely for all $z\in\mathbb{R}$, $\left|\sup_{x\in[x_0+A,x_0+A+2]} \hz{z_1}(x) - \sup_{x\in[x_0+A,x_0+A+2]} \hz{z_2}(x)\right|$ is at most $2|z_1-z_2|$ (from Lemma~\ref{l.lipschitz}). We apply this to $z_1 = \mathrm{Corner}^{\uparrow}$ and $z_2\in I_\varepsilon$.


With this preparation, we see that

\begin{align}
\MoveEqLeft[12]
\mathbb P\left(\sup_{x\in [x_0+A,x_0+A+2]} \mathfrak{h}^{{\scriptscriptstyle(}n{\scriptscriptstyle)}}(x) > \mathfrak{h}^{{\scriptscriptstyle(}n{\scriptscriptstyle)}}(x_0) - \varepsilon\ \bigg|\ \mathscr{F}\right)\mathbbm{1}_{|\mathfrak{h}^{{\scriptscriptstyle(}n{\scriptscriptstyle)}}(x_0)|\leq \beta L^{1/2},\, |x_0|\leq \beta L-A-2}\nonumber\\

&\geq \mathbb P\left(\sup_{x\in [x_0+A,x_0+A+2]} \mathfrak{h}^{{\scriptscriptstyle(}n{\scriptscriptstyle)}}(x) > \mathfrak{h}^{{\scriptscriptstyle(}n{\scriptscriptstyle)}}(x_0) - \varepsilon\ \bigg|\ \mathscr{F}\right)\cdot \mathbbm{1}_{\mathsf{Fav}}\nonumber\\

&\geq \mathbb P\big(Z \in I_{\varepsilon}\ \big|\ \mathscr{F}\big)\cdot \mathbbm{1}_{\mathsf{Fav}} . \label{e.Z in interval prob}

\end{align}

Recall now from Lemma~\ref{l.conditional distribution} that $Z$ is distributed as a normal random variable with mean $\mu = \frac{1}{2}(\mathcal{P}_{n,1}(x_0+A) + \mathcal{P}_{n,1}(x_0+A+2))$ and variance one, conditioned on lying inside $[\mathrm{Corner}^{\downarrow}, \mathrm{Corner}^{\uparrow}]$. Observe from \eqref{e.I_epsilon} that $I_\varepsilon$ is one of two intervals: $[\mathrm{Corner}^{\downarrow}, \mathrm{Corner}^{\uparrow}]$ or $[\mathrm{Corner}^{\uparrow}-\varepsilon/2, \mathrm{Corner}^{\uparrow}]$. In the first case, the conditional probability in \eqref{e.Z in interval prob} equals one. We show now that, in the second case, the conditional probability is bounded below by $c'\varepsilon$ for some constant $c'>0$.

We let $N$ be a standard normal random variable with mean zero and variance one. Then, on the event $\mathsf{Fav}\cap\{\mathrm{Corner}^{\downarrow} < \mathrm{Corner}^{\uparrow}-\varepsilon/2\}$, we have that $|\mu| \leq K$ and $\mathrm{Corner}^{\uparrow} \leq 4K$, which implies that, on the same event,

\begin{align*}
\mathbb P\big(Z \in I_\varepsilon\ \big|\ \mathscr{F}\big)

&= \mathbb P\left(N +\mu \in [\mathrm{Corner}^{\uparrow} -\varepsilon/2, \mathrm{Corner}^{\uparrow}]\  \Big|\  N+\mu \in [\mathrm{Corner}^{\downarrow}, \mathrm{Corner}^{\uparrow}], \mathscr{F}\right)\\

&= \frac{\mathbb P\left(N +\mu \in [\mathrm{Corner}^{\uparrow} -\varepsilon/2, \mathrm{Corner}^{\uparrow}]\  \Big|\ \mathscr{F}\right)}{\mathbb P\left(N+\mu \in [\mathrm{Corner}^{\downarrow}, \mathrm{Corner}^{\uparrow}]\  \Big|\   \mathscr{F}\right)}\\

&\geq \mathbb P\left(N+\mu \geq \mathrm{Corner}^{\uparrow} -\varepsilon/2 \  \Big|\  N+\mu \leq \mathrm{Corner}^{\uparrow}, \mathscr{F}\right)\\

&\geq \mathbb P\left(N +\mu  \geq 4K -\varepsilon/2\  \Big|\ N+\mu \leq 4K, \mathscr{F}\right)\\

&\geq  \mathbb P\big(N +\mu  \in [4K -\varepsilon/2, 4K]\ \big|\ \mathscr{F}\big).
\end{align*}

For the first equality, we interpret $\mathbb P(Z\in \cdot \mid \mathscr{F})$ as a regular conditional distribution, which exists as $Z$ takes values in $\mathbb{R}$ (see \cite[Theorem~6.3]{Kallenberg}); conditioning on an event $E$  is then understood by the usual equality of conditional probability with a ratio of probabilities, i.e., $\mathbb P(\cdot \mid E, \mathscr{F}) = \mathbb P(\cdot\cap E\mid \mathscr{F})/\mathbb P(E\mid \mathscr{F})$. Then the first equality follows from the characterization of $Z$'s law recalled above after \eqref{e.Z in interval prob}. The second equality can be seen by noting that we are working on the event that $\mathrm{Corner}^\downarrow < \mathrm{Corner}^\uparrow-\varepsilon/2$, and some simple manipulations of the probabilities in the ratio gives the third line, i.e., the first inequality.
The penultimate inequality used the monotonicity property of normal random variables recorded in Lemma~\ref{l.normal monotonicity} and that $\mathrm{Corner}^{\uparrow}\leq 4K$ on $\mathsf{Fav}$. Now the form of the normal density gives that the final expression is bounded below by $c'\varepsilon\cdot\mathbbm{1}_{\mathsf{Fav}}$ for some $c'>0$ depending only on $K$, since $|\mu|\leq K$; further, this dependence is clearly continuous in $K$.

Substituting  into \eqref{e.Z in interval prob} this bound, as well as the earlier bound of one in the case that $\mathrm{Corner}^{\downarrow}\geq \mathrm{Corner}^{\uparrow}-\varepsilon/2$, gives that

\begin{align*}
\MoveEqLeft[24]
\mathbb P\left(\sup_{x\in [x_0+A,x_0+A+2]} \mathfrak{h}^{{\scriptscriptstyle(}n{\scriptscriptstyle)}}(x) > \mathfrak{h}^{{\scriptscriptstyle(}n{\scriptscriptstyle)}}(x_0) - \varepsilon;\, |\mathfrak{h}^{{\scriptscriptstyle(}n{\scriptscriptstyle)}}(x_0)| \leq \beta L; \, |x_0|\leq \beta L-A-2\right)\\

&\geq c'\varepsilon\cdot \mathbb P\big(\mathsf{Fav}_{K,L}\big) \geq \frac{1}{2}c' \varepsilon,
\end{align*}

in view of $K$ and $L$ being such that $\mathbb P(\mathsf{Fav}_{K,L}) \geq 1/2$. Relabelling $c'$ completes the proof of Proposition~\ref{p.resampling twin peaks}.

Now the form of the normal density gives that the final expression is bounded below by c'varepsiloncdotmathbbm1_Fav for some c'>0 depending only on K, since |mu|leq K; further, this dependence is clearly continuous in K. Relabelling c' completes the proof of Proposition~.

nodes.statement: thmtitleHausdorff measure and dimension Let S subset R and 0 leq alpha < infty. item For 0 < delta leq infty, we define the delta-approximate packing pre-measure H^alpha_delta(S) := inf left\ sum_i = 1^infty diam (J_i)^alpha : S subset bigcup_i = 1^infty J_i,\; diam (J_i) < delta right\, where the infimum is taken over all countable covers of S by sets J_i subset R with diam(J_i) < delta, and where diam(J_i) is the supremum of all distances between points in J_i. item We define the alpha-dimensional Hausdorff measure H^alpha(S) := lim_delta to 0 H^alpha_delta(S) = sup_delta > 0 H^alpha_delta(S). We note that H^alpha(S) is well-defined (although it can be infinite), because H^alpha_delta(S) monotonically increases as delta searrow 0. item The Hausdorff dimension of S is defined by the following equivalent formulas: dim(S) &:= sup \alpha geq 0 : H^alpha(S) > 0\ = sup \alpha geq 0 : H^alpha(S) = infty\ \\ &= inf \alpha geq 0 : H^alpha(S) < infty\ = inf \alpha geq 0 : H^alpha(S) = 0\. Note that 0 leq dim(S) leq 1 for any S subset R.
